chunks: And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, who said:

He said regarding the traveler who enters to his family in the month of Ramadan and has eaten before entering: He should refrain from eating for the remainder of the day, and upon him is the making up (of the fast).

And he said regarding the traveler who enters to his family while he is in a state of major ritual impurity before midday, and he had not eaten: It is upon him to complete his fast, and there is no making up upon him, meaning if his impurity was from a nocturnal emission.

key_terms.الجُنُبُ: One in a state of major ritual impurity
key_terms.الزَّوَالُ: Midday (when the sun begins to decline)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a traveler who returns home during Ramadan having eaten or being in a state of major impurity?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani's al-Ishtibār clarifies the distinction between breaking the fast due to consumption versus the state of ritual impurity (junub) upon a traveler's return. It establishes that if the traveler has not eaten, his state of major impurity does not invalidate the fast, provided the impurity resulted from a natural emission (ihtilam) rather than sexual intercourse, reflecting the Shia juristic view that junub is not a nullifier of fasting itself. This ruling underscores the practical ease granted to travelers while maintaining the integrity of the Ramadan obligation.
